summary: Tenant token drain caused by rate-window collisions during orchestrated ingest workers
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports sudden exhaustion of tenant token budget (429s) during an orchestrated ingest job that runs many short-lived worker tasks in parallel. Problem appears only after a recent change to their orchestrator which stitches multiple short-lived upload workers together into waves.

Impact: Intermittent 429s for interactive routes and bulk ingest pipelines for NimbleAI; visible around the top of each orchestrated wave. Client reports degraded throughput and a spike in retries. No model-level errors observed.

Environment: Dedicated pool in prod-us-west; tenant pinned to dedicated lease. Ingest job spawns 120 workers, each opening short-lived streaming sessions and issuing small embed/chat requests.

Steps to reproduce (provided by customer):
1) Trigger nightly orchestrated backfill with 120 parallel workers.
2) Each worker opens a new short-lived API connection, completes a 6-12 request burst, then terminates.
3) Observe tenant-level 429s starting ~60s after wave start, continuing until refill stabilization.

Observed logs (snippets):
[2026-03-09T02:14:32Z] auth-service: token-grant OK tenant=nbl-231;
[2026-03-09T02:14:59Z] rate-limiter: REJECT tenant=nbl-231 window=60s tokens_left=0 reason=burst-window-exhausted;
[2026-03-09T02:15:01Z] gateway: 429 path=/v1/embeddings size=512 host=ingest-worker-77;

Additional context: Customer recently enabled orchestrator-level parallelism optimization (stagger disabled) and moved orchestration to a single coordinator to reduce scheduling churn. They also requested a single burst pool for both low-latency chat and large background batches to reduce operational complexity.

Why this is unique: The patterns indicate a shed/"shearing" effect where many short-lived sessions align to refill boundaries and create transient window collisions that exhaust tenant burst credits faster than steady-state smoothing anticipates. This is different from long-lived SSE or healthcheck-induced 429s because the traffic is high-cardinality, short-duration, and aligned with the orchestrator's wave timing.
investigation_notes:
Hypotheses: 1) Refill window alignment lets multiple workers consume the same refill credit slice; 2) Token slicing at API-gateway is attributing requests twice on worker restart; 3) Dedicated-pool refill lag during autoscaler scale-up is delaying credit replenishment.

Telemetry collected:
- Rate-controller histograms show refill bursts at t+0s and t+60s for the tenant; cumulative consumption spikes when worker start times are within the same 10s bucket.
- Dedicated pool autoscaler logs show scale-up completed but serving nodes not fully warmed; kernel-level warmup delays add ~200ms per connection.
- Gateway logs confirm ephemeral worker connections are reusing different source IPs (NAT pool), increasing header fingerprint variance and preventing per-connection affinity counting.

Notes from quick checks:
- Reproduced in staging with a synthetic orchestrator using 100 short-lived workers; 429 pattern matches production traces.
- Turning on stagger (small jitter on worker start) reduces peak token drain by ~40% in staging.

Relevant dashboards: 
- https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/rate-ctrl/tenant-consumption?orgId=1&var-tenant=nbl-231
- https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/infra/dedicated-pool-warmup?orgId=1

Next investigative actions: capture exact refill window alignment, check gateway token attribution code path for worker reconnects, and reproduce varying stagger/jitter to quantify mitigation.
comments: 2026-03-10 - Ava Martinez (Support): Created ticket after NimbleAI pinged #support with 429 wave traces and request for guidance. Attached initial logs and Grafana links.

2026-03-10 - Jacob Lee (NimbleAI): We flipped orchestrator staggers off on 2026-03-08 to reduce job time. Since then we've seen the waves. Happy to test any config change.
Logs: s3://nimble-logs/ingest/2026-03-09/trace.log

2026-03-11 - Diego Chen (SRE): Confirmed reproduction in staging. Early observation: peak alignment of worker-start events falls inside our 60s refill window; staggering start times looks promising. Will instrument gateway to record per-connection token attribution on next run.

2026-03-12 - Priya Nair (Platform Eng): Noted a potential double-count when ephemeral worker does a connection restart and preflight. Proposed patch to idempotently tag in-flight worker sessions (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/879).

2026-03-12 - Jacob Lee (NimbleAI): We've enabled a temporary orchestrator jitter (200-800ms) and reduced concurrent worker bursts while you debug. Observed fewer 429s during the subsequent backfill run.
workaround:
Short-term: enable small start jitter (200-1000ms) for orchestrated workers to spread token consumption across refill windows; separate background-batch tenant route into a dedicated burst pool (request via console -> create burst pool). Both actions reduced 429s in staging.

Customer-applied config: NimbleAI enabled 500ms jitter and created a background-batch route assigned to a separate burst pool; reported immediate throughput improvement.
resolution:
Mitigation provided (stagger + route separation) and engineering patch under review to make gateway token attribution idempotent for ephemeral connections. Pending: PR for edge-proxy session-tagging (https://github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/879) and a follow-up to expose 'orchestrator-jitter' recommendations in Console docs.

Follow-up tasks: 1) Merge and roll PR to staging and run full repro; 2) Add a Console toggle for 'orchestrator jitter' recommendations under dedicated-pool best practices; 3) Document guidance for splitting burst pools for mixed-latency workloads (assigned to Diego Chen).
notes_for_ops: If customer cannot apply jitter, consider temporarily increasing tenant burst-window size for dedicated lease (admin action) and coordinate with billing (burst credit implications). Use rate-controller debug mode to watch per-window attribution.
customer_communication_summary: Explained root cause hypothesis (window collision from many short-lived worker starts), provided two low-friction mitigations (start jitter + separate burst pool), and delivered short-term improvement. Customer is awaiting platform-side fix for safer ephemeral-session handling.
